questions.stem: State the energy transferred expression and the value used for c in aqueous calorimetry.
questions.modelAnswer: q = m x c x delta-T, with c taken as 4.18 J g^-1 K^-1 for dilute aqueous solutions.
keywords: q = m x c x delta-T

questions.stem: List the assumptions made when treating the solution as water in the calculation.
questions.modelAnswer: The solution's density is 1 g cm^-3 (so its volume equals its mass in grams) and its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g^-1 K^-1.

questions.stem: Explain why the zinc powder is used in excess in the displacement method.
questions.modelAnswer: Excess zinc guarantees every mole of copper sulfate reacts, so the limiting reagent's known mole count cleanly divides the measured energy for the per-mole answer.

questions.stem: A neutralisation between 40.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide and 35.0 cm3 of sulfuric acid warms the mixture by 9.5 degrees. Taking the combined solution mass and c = 4.18, compute q.
questions.modelAnswer: The combined mass is 40.0 + 35.0 = 75.0 g, so q = 75.0 x 4.18 x 9.5 = 2978 J of energy transferred to the solution.

questions.stem: Describe the temperature correction graph procedure in three steps.
questions.modelAnswer: Record temperature every half minute before and after mixing, extrapolate both lines back to the time of mixing, and read the corrected temperature change at that intersection.

questions.stem: Explain, in one sentence, why two trend lines are needed on the correction graph.
questions.modelAnswer: The pre-mixing line fixes the baseline and the post-mixing line carries the leak, so their extrapolation back to the mixing time gives the zero-loss reading.

questions.stem: Explain why the correction increases rather than decreases the measured temperature change.
questions.modelAnswer: The uncorrected peak already lost heat to the room, so rewinding the leak adds the missing energy back and widens the measured gap.

questions.stem: A temperature correction graph shows the cooling line falling 0.4 degrees per half minute. State what happens to the corrected change if the leak rate doubles.
questions.modelAnswer: The extrapolated correction doubles in size, so the corrected temperature change grows by the extra 0.4 degrees per half minute back-projected to the mixing time.

questions.stem: State the full procedure for measuring an enthalpy change of combustion.
questions.modelAnswer: Weigh the burner, burn the fuel beneath a known mass of water recording the temperature rise, reweigh the burner, then compute q = m x c x delta-T and divide by the moles of fuel burned, giving the negative molar value.

questions.stem: State the direction of the systematic error in combustion calorimetry and its cause.
questions.modelAnswer: The measured value is less negative than the true one, because heat escapes to the air before the water can capture it.

questions.stem: Explain why the combustion enthalpy carries a negative sign by definition.
questions.modelAnswer: Combustion releases energy to the surroundings, so the system's enthalpy falls and the products-minus-reactants difference is negative.

questions.stem: A burner loses 0.92 g of methanol and the water gains 18.6 kJ. Taking the molar mass of methanol as 32 g mol-1, calculate the measured enthalpy of combustion.
questions.modelAnswer: Moles burned = 0.92 / 32 = 0.0288 mol, so the enthalpy change is -18.6 / 0.0288 = -646 kJ mol-1 (approximately), the negative sign recording the energy release.
